introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer FOUR questions in all. Answer question ONE and three others, choosing ONE question from SECTION B and TWO from SECTION C. Question ONE carries thirty-one marks and the rest carry twenty-three marks each.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Candidates are advised NOT to attempt the questions on field investigations if such an exercise has not been carried out.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and two outline maps of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Describe the differences in the relief characteristics north of northing 39. (4 marks)

(ii) Briefly comment on the relationship between relief and drainage in the map area north of northing 39. (5 marks)

(iii) Calculate the Sinuosity Index of River Nun along the section between points "A" at 632425 and "B" at 650397. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a)(i) Differences in relief north of northing 39 (4 marks).** Describe the relief by sectors, using contour spacing, spot heights and grid references, and contrast them (high/low, steep/gentle, rugged/flat).

- **West and north-west (about eastings 50 to 58).** The land is high and rugged. Contours are close together, so slopes are steep; there are hills with closed, concentric contours and an east-west ridge or escarpment (a band of very dense brown contours) around northing 41. Valleys are narrow and V-shaped between the hills.
- **Centre-north (about eastings 55 to 59).** The ground is undulating, with gentler slopes (wider contour spacing) and a few isolated hills rising above a low surface.
- **East and north-east (about eastings 59 to 65).** The land is low, flat and almost featureless: contours are very widely spaced or absent, spot heights are close to one another (of the order of 1,140 m on the plain), and the ground is swampy. Only isolated hills, such as the one just north of Ndop, break the flatness.
- **General trend.** The ground falls from the high rugged country in the west and north-west to the low plain in the east and north-east (the Ndop plain), so the relief contrast is between a dissected hilly area and a flat alluvial plain.

(Quote at least two spot heights or contour values from the original sheet to support the contrast.)

**(a)(ii) Relief and drainage (5 marks).**
- **Source areas and direction of flow.** Streams rise on the higher ground in the west and north-west and flow down the slope towards the low-lying east and north-east, where they join the River Nun. The drainage pattern therefore follows the general slope of the land.
- **On the hills.** Slopes are steep, so streams are short, fast, straight and cut narrow V-shaped valleys; contours bend upstream (V pointing uphill) where they cross a valley. Many small streams and valleys occur, so drainage density is higher.
- **On the plain.** The gradient is very gentle, so the River Nun flows slowly, with a wide, flat valley floor and an irregular, winding channel. Tributaries are fewer, there are intermittent streams, and large areas are swampy (the swampy-land symbol) because water drains poorly and the channel cannot evacuate it quickly. The sinuous course of the Nun on the flat ground reflects the lack of relief.
- **Conclusion.** Relief controls the direction of flow, the density and the pattern of the drainage: steep ground gives many short straight streams; flat ground gives a slow, winding river and marshes.

**(a)(iii) Sinuosity Index (3 marks).**

Formula:

$$
SI=\dfrac{\text{actual channel length}}{\text{straight-line distance between the two points}}
$$

1. Locate the points. A = 632425 means easting 63.2, northing 42.5; B = 650397 means easting 65.0, northing 39.7. Grid lines are 1 km apart (2 cm on the map at 1:50,000).
2. Straight-line distance: difference in easting $= 65.0 - 63.2 = 1.8$ km; difference in northing $= 42.5 - 39.7 = 2.8$ km. By Pythagoras, $d=\sqrt{1.8^2+2.8^2}=\sqrt{11.08}\approx 3.3$ km (about 6.7 cm on the map).
3. Channel length: lay a thread along the winding river from A to B, straighten it and read it against the scale. On the reproduction printed here the channel measures about 4 km (about 8 cm on the original map). Candidates' own measurements may differ slightly; the method carries the marks.
4. Calculation: $SI=\dfrac{4.0}{3.3}\approx 1.2$.
5. Interpretation: a value of 1.0 is a perfectly straight channel; values between about 1.05 and 1.5 indicate a sinuous channel; above about 1.5 the river is meandering. An index of about 1.2 shows a moderately sinuous channel on a very gentle gradient, consistent with the low, swampy plain.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Describe and account for:

(i) the location of rice farms/plantations. (4 marks)

(ii) the distribution of road network. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(b)(i) Location of rice farms/plantations (4 marks).**

*Description.* Using the rice-plantation symbol of the key (a dotted pattern), rice is found on the **flat, low-lying, poorly drained ground of the Ndop plain**, near the swampy valley floors, in blocks of regularly laid out plots close to settlements and roads, for example the dotted rectangular blocks south-east of Balikumbat (about grid squares 56-57 / 36, as read on the reproduction). Candidates must quote grid references read from the original sheet. The rice farms are absent from the steep, hilly western and north-western parts.

*Account.*
- **Relief.** The flat ground allows the plots to be levelled and bunded and the water to be controlled.
- **Water.** Swampy or seasonally flooded land and the nearby River Nun provide the water that paddy rice needs; irrigation canals can be fed from the river.
- **Soils.** The alluvial and hydromorphic soils of the plain retain water and are fertile.
- **Accessibility and labour.** The farms are near villages (a ready labour force) and near roads, which carry the paddy to the mill and the market at Ndop.
- **Organisation.** The regular layout points to a planned scheme; the Ndop plain is the site of the state rice project of the Upper Nun Valley Development Authority (UNVDA), set up in the 1970s.

**(b)(ii) Distribution of the road network (4 marks).**

*Description.* The road network is **uneven**. A tarred road crosses the north of the map from the north-west, passes through the Bamessing area and reaches **Ndop**, the main node, then continues eastwards. Earth roads radiate from Ndop and from the other larger settlements (Bamessing, Bamali, Balikumbat, Bamukumbit) and link them; the density of roads is highest around the settlements and over the flat central and eastern plain. The hilly west and north-west and the swampy ground have few roads and are served only by footpaths.

*Account.*
- **Relief.** Roads are cheaper to build on the flat plain and tend to follow valley floors or gentle slopes; steep, dissected hills and swamps are avoided (or crossed by footpaths).
- **Settlement pattern.** Roads join the nucleated settlements and radiate from the town that is the commercial and administrative centre (Ndop).
- **Economic activities.** Roads evacuate farm produce, notably rice, to the market.
- **Investment.** The state tars the main axis that links the area to the regional capital and to other towns, while villages use earth roads built and maintained locally.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Draw a topological diagram of the transport network linking the following settlements shown on the map: Ndop, Bamessing, Bamali, Balikumbat, Bamukumbit and Bafanji. (4 marks)

(ii) Calculate the Beta Index of the network shown in (c)(i) above. (2 marks)

(iii) What is the significance of your result? (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(c)(i) Topological diagram (4 marks).** A topological diagram is a simplified sketch in which each settlement is a **vertex (node)** and each direct road link is an **edge (link)**; distances, directions and road quality are ignored. Read from the map which of the six settlements are directly joined by a road (without passing through another of the six), then draw the vertices as small circles, label them and join them with straight lines.

A model diagram, based on the roads read on the reproduction of the map, joins Ndop to Bamessing and to Bamali, Bamessing to Bamali, Bamali to Balikumbat, and Balikumbat to Bamukumbit and to Bafanji:

![fig-3](gce-al-geography-2019-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

(The exact set of links depends on the candidate's reading of the map; the marks are for correct vertices, labels, edges only between directly linked settlements and a neat, unscaled diagram.)

**(c)(ii) Beta Index (2 marks).**

$$
\beta=\dfrac{e}{v}
$$

where $e$ is the number of edges and $v$ the number of vertices. For the model network, $v = 6$ and $e = 6$, so $\beta=\dfrac{6}{6}=1.0$. (A candidate who counts $e=5$ gets $\beta = 5/6 \approx 0.83$; $e=7$ gives about $1.17$: the working is marked consistently with the diagram drawn.)

**(c)(iii) Significance (1 mark).** A tree-like network has $\beta<1$, a network with exactly one circuit has $\beta=1$, and $\beta>1$ shows several circuits (for a planar network with six vertices the maximum is $3(v-2)/v = 2.0$). A value of 1.0 means that the network is only moderately connected: every settlement can be reached and there is one alternative route (a single circuit among Ndop, Bamessing and Bamali), but the southern settlements depend on single links, so the network is simple and not fully developed; more roads would increase connectivity and accessibility.

questions.enonce_markdown: (d) Briefly describe the site and situation of Ndop. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Site** is the actual ground on which the town is built; **situation** is its position in relation to the surrounding area and other places.

*Site (2 marks).* Ndop lies in the north-east of the map extract (about grid square 60 / 44). It is built on low, flat to gently sloping ground at the edge of the Ndop plain, at the foot of a hill that rises just to the north-west, with the swampy valley of the River Nun a few kilometres to the east. The ground is above the swampy floor, so it is better drained and dry enough for building, while the plain gives space to expand and fertile land (rice and other crops) for its farmers.

*Situation (2 marks).* Ndop lies in the Ndop plain, a basin in the Grassfields of the North-West Region. It stands on the tarred road that comes from the north-west and continues east, and at the meeting point of the earth roads to the surrounding villages (Bamessing, Bamali, Bamunka, Balikumbat and others), so it is the nodal and market centre of the area, with the surrounding hills forming a ring around the plain.
